p: Later manuscripts and the KJV add 'through the Spirit'.

readings.w: P72, Sinaiticus (01, 300s), Alexandrinus (02, 400s), Vaticanus (03, 300s), C (04), Ψ, 33, 81, 323, 945, 1241, 1739, the Latin Vulgate, Syriac and Coptic versions; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT

readings.en: by obedience to the truth through the Spirit
readings.plain: Your obedience to the truth through the Spirit

why: The oldest and most varied witnesses lack the phrase. It looks like an addition that names the Holy Spirit as the one who purifies, as in 1:2.

t: "From a pure heart" or "from the heart"?
p: Some important manuscripts lack 'pure'; one corrector wrote 'a true heart'.

readings.w: P72, Sinaiticus as first written (01*), C (04), P, Ψ, 33, 1739, the majority of manuscripts, Coptic versions; NA28 (printed with a diamond, marking a close call), THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), 1852, the Latin Vulgate; SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
A later corrector of Sinaiticus (01, second hand), some Vulgate manuscripts

why: The word has early and widespread support, including P72. A copyist could have dropped it by skipping between the two similar endings (katharas kardias). The NET Bible's note calls it the likely original, and NA28 follows it. SBL omits it, so this is one of the places where this site follows NA28 against the SBL text.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add 'forever', as in the Isaiah quotation two verses later.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'which liveth and abideth for ever')

why: The added words match 'remains forever' in 1:25, and copyists tended to make such phrases match. The editions that weigh the oldest manuscripts leave them out.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'all the glory of man', as the Greek of Isaiah 40:6 does.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'all the glory of man')

why: The Greek of Isaiah 40:6 (in Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete) has 'the glory of man'. A copyist who knew Isaiah could easily change Peter's 'its glory' to match; the reverse is less likely. The same Byzantine text also adds 'its' to 'the flower' at the end of the verse.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV lack 'into salvation'.

readings.w: P72, Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), C (04), K, P, Ψ, 33, 81, 630, 1241, 1505, 1739 and others, the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'that ye may grow thereby')

why: The words have very early and broad support. Copyists may have dropped them because 'growing into salvation' seemed to make salvation something earned by growth, as the NET Bible's note suggests.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'those who disobey'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: to those who do not believe

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'unto them which be disobedient')

why: The critical editions read 'disbelieve', which answers 'you who believe' at the start of the verse. The other reading matches 'refusing to obey' in 2:8 and 'refuse to obey' in 3:1 and 4:17, and a copyist could have changed one word to the other in either direction. The two Greek words look alike.

p: The unusual phrase 'conscience of God' was changed in several ways by copyists.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), a corrector of Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), P, 049, 5, 436, 1735, the majority of manuscripts, Latin and Coptic versions; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
P72, Alexandrinus as first written (02*), 33, 81, 2344
readings.en: because of a good conscience of God
readings.plain: out of a good conscience toward God

why: 'Conscience of God' occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, so copyists changed it to the familiar 'good conscience' (as in 3:16, 21). The harder phrase best explains the others, and it has strong support.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'suffered for us'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'Christ also suffered for us')

why: The Greek words for 'you' and 'us' (hymon, hemon) sounded alike and are often confused in the manuscripts. Peter is speaking to slaves ('you were called'), so 'for you' fits; 'for us' makes it a general confession.

a: as to co-heirs with you of the grace of life
p: In some texts the wives are co-heirs; in others the husbands are, together with their wives.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Tregelles
readings.plain: as to co-heirs with you of the grace of life

readings.w: Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'as being heirs together of the grace of life')
readings.en: as also co-heirs (the husbands, with their wives)
readings.plain: as men who are co-heirs together of the grace of life

why: The difference is one letter (dative -ois or nominative -oi). The dative makes the honor owed to wives rest on their being equal heirs; the nominative makes husbands and wives heirs together. The meaning is close either way.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'courteous' (philophrones) for 'humble' (tapeinophrones).

Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'be courteous')

why: The two words differ in their first part only. Humility is a theme of the letter (5:5-6), which fits the critical text.

p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus add 'knowing that' before 'you were called'.

why: The critical editions all lack the word. 'Knowing that' is the kind of small link copyists added to smooth a sentence; the meaning hardly changes.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'followers (imitators) of what is good'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'followers of that which is good')

why: 'Imitators' is a word Paul often uses (1 Corinthians 11:1), and a copyist may have brought it in. The meaning is little changed.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'sanctify the Lord God in your hearts'.

readings.w: P72, Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), C (04), Ψ, 33, 1175, 1243, 1611, 1739, 1852, the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
P, 5, 81, 436, 442, 1735, 2344, 2492, the majority of manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'sanctify the Lord God')

why: 'Christ' has the earliest and widest support. 'The Lord God' is the far more common phrase in the Bible, and it brings the verse back in line with Isaiah 8:13, where the LORD is to be counted holy.

a: for which you are spoken against
t: "You are spoken against" or "they speak against you as wrongdoers"?
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add 'as wrongdoers', from 2:12.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: in what you are spoken against
readings.plain: for which you are spoken against

readings.en: in what they speak against you as wrongdoers
readings.plain: for which they speak against you as wrongdoers

why: The longer form repeats the wording of 2:12 almost exactly, and copyists often made similar verses match.

p: Many important manuscripts read 'died for sins'.

readings.w: Vaticanus (03), L, P, 81, 2492, the majority of manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus

why: The manuscripts are evenly matched, and the NET Bible's note says the outside evidence slightly favors 'died'. 'Suffered' fits the context: 3:14 and 3:17 speak of suffering, and 4:1 says 'Christ, then, suffered in the flesh'. Copyists familiar with the creed 'Christ died for our sins' (1 Corinthians 15:3) would easily change 'suffered' to 'died'. The NET note reports that Metzger's Textual Commentary lists eight different readings in this verse.

p: The Textus Receptus and the KJV read 'that he might bring us to God'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text
readings.en: so that he could lead you to God

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV 'that he might bring us to God')
readings.en: so that he could lead us to God

why: As in 2:21, 'you' and 'us' are easily confused. Peter is addressing his readers directly.

p: The Textus Receptus splits one Greek word into two, 'once waited', which is the KJV's 'when once the longsuffering of God waited'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (Stephanus 1550, Scrivener 1894; KJV 'when once the longsuffering of God waited')

why: Every critical edition and the Byzantine text have the single word apexedecheto, 'was waiting'. The Textus Receptus reads hapax exedecheto, 'once waited', a different division of nearly the same letters. The verse already says 'once, long ago' (pote), so the sense is close.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'saves us'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'baptism doth also now save us')

why: Again 'you' and 'us'. The meaning is the same; the KJV's 'us' made the verse a general statement about all believers.

p: Many manuscripts and the KJV add 'for us' (some 'for you').

why: The shortest reading has early support and explains the others: copyists added 'for us' or 'for you' to echo 2:21 and 3:18. The NET Bible's note strongly prefers it.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add 'of our life' and 'for us'.

readings.plain: The time already gone by was plenty

why: The added words make the sentence smoother and include the writer ('us'); the shorter text is the one the critical editions print. The Byzantine text also reads thelema, 'will', for boulema, 'what they want', with the same meaning.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read the future, 'will cover' ('shall cover').

Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'charity shall cover the multitude of sins')

why: The present matches Proverbs 10:12, which states a general truth. The future may come from James 5:20, which has 'will lay a cover'.

t: "Of glory" or "of glory and of power"?
p: Many manuscripts add 'and of power'. The evidence is evenly divided.

readings.w: P72, Vaticanus (03), K, L, Ψ, 049 and about half the later manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
Sinaiticus (01, with a small difference), Alexandrinus (02), P, 33, 81, 323, 945, 1241, 1739 and about half the later manuscripts, Bohairic Coptic
readings.en: the [Spirit] of glory and of power
readings.plain: the Spirit of glory and of power

why: The witnesses are evenly divided. The longer reading looks like an explanatory or liturgical expansion (glory and power often go together, as in 4:11), as the NET Bible's note judges.

t: A sentence added in the Byzantine text
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add 'On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified')
readings.orig: ἐφ᾽ ὑμᾶς ἀναπαύεται· κατὰ μὲν αὐτοὺς βλασφημεῖται, κατὰ δὲ ὑμᾶς δοξάζεται
readings.en: rests on you; on their side he is slandered, but on your side he is glorified
readings.plain: comes to rest on you. On their side he is slandered, but on your side he is glorified

why: The sentence is missing from the editions that weigh the oldest manuscripts. It reads like a comment written in the margin to explain the verse, which later entered the text.

p: Here NA28 and the Editio Critica Maior changed the text that NA27 and SBL print.

readings.w: NA28 and the Editio Critica Maior (2013), Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'on this behalf')
readings.en: in this matter, in this respect

readings.w: NA27, SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

why: The Editio Critica Maior, the large critical edition of the Catholic Letters, changed the reading from 'name' to 'matter', and NA28 adopted it; the change was based on the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method, the computer-assisted way of tracing how manuscripts are related. The change has been questioned (for example by Kobus Kok and Bastiaan de Winter in 2017), and SBL and THGNT keep 'name'. 'Name' fits 'the name of Christ' (4:14) and 'Christian' so well that a copyist could have brought it in, which is one argument for 'matter'. The site follows NA28 here, as it does in the Catholic Letters where NA28 and SBL differ.
b: Only editions are listed here. The manuscript evidence for this change is set out in the Editio Critica Maior's apparatus; the abstract of Kok and de Winter's article describes the debate.

t: "So, to the elders" or "To the elders"?
p: NA28 reads 'the elders among you' with no 'so'; SBL and older critical editions read 'So, to the elders'.

readings.w: NA28, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'The elders which are among you I exhort')
readings.en: the elders who are among you

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA27, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: So, to the elders among you

readings.w: THGNT
readings.plain: So, to the elders among you

why: NA28 differs here from SBL and from NA27, and in the Catholic Letters the site follows NA28 where the two differ. The difference is a small linking word ('so', oun) and the article ('the'); the meaning is the same.

t: "Overseeing it": in most manuscripts, missing in two early ones
p: Codex Sinaiticus as first written and Codex Vaticanus lack 'overseeing it'.

readings.w: P72, a corrector of Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), P, Ψ, 33, 1739, the majority of manuscripts, Latin and Bohairic Coptic versions; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
Sinaiticus as first written (01*), Vaticanus (03), Sahidic Coptic; Westcott-Hort

why: The word has wide and early support. The NET Bible's note suggests that the omission may come from copyists who hesitated to link 'oversight' (the work later given to bishops) with elders.

t: "In God's way": missing in the KJV
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV lack 'according to God'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Tregelles
Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'but willingly')

why: The critical editions differ here: SBL, NA28, THGNT and Tregelles print the words, Westcott-Hort and the Byzantine text lack them. Kata theon can mean 'as God wants' or 'in a godly way'.

p: The Textus Receptus and the KJV read 'who hath called us'.

Textus Receptus (KJV 'who hath called us')

why: As elsewhere in the letter, 'you' and 'us' were easily confused; the Byzantine text agrees with the critical editions here.

p: Most manuscripts add 'Jesus'; NA28 marks the choice as a close call.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), 614, 630, 1505, 1611; SBLGNT, NA28 (with a diamond), THGNT
P72, Alexandrinus (02), P, Ψ, 5, 33, 81, 436, 442, 1175, 1735, 1739, 1852, 2344, 2492, the majority of manuscripts, Latin versions; NA27, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus

why: The longer reading has broad and early support, but adding 'Jesus' to 'Christ' was a natural expansion. NA28 prints the shorter text with a diamond in the apparatus, marking it as a toss-up, and the NET Bible's note calls the decision difficult.

a: give you strength and lay a foundation under you
p: Two nineteenth-century editions leave out the last verb, 'lay a foundation'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Byzantine text (the Textus Receptus has the same verbs in the form of a wish: KJV 'make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you')
readings.en: he will strengthen, he will found
readings.plain: give you strength and lay a foundation under you

readings.w: Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

why: The current critical editions all print the fourth verb. The Textus Receptus also reads the first verb as a wish ('may he restore you'), so the KJV reads the verse as a prayer.

p: NA28 reads 'forever'; SBL and the Byzantine text 'forever and ever'; the KJV adds 'the glory and'.

readings.w: NA28 (and NA27)
SBLGNT, THGNT, Tregelles

t: "Stand in it" or "in which you stand"?
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'wherein ye stand', a statement instead of a command.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'the true grace of God wherein ye stand')

why: The command fits the letter's many calls to stand firm (5:9). The perfect 'you stand' may echo Romans 5:2, 'this grace where we now stand'.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV end 'in Christ Jesus. Amen.'

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV 'in Christ Jesus. Amen')

why: Copyists routinely added 'Amen' at the end of New Testament books, and the early witnesses that lack it are hard to explain if it was there from the start, as the NET Bible's note says. 'Jesus' is found in the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus but not in the critical editions.
b: On 'Amen' alone, the NET Bible's note lists P72, Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), Ψ, 81, 323, 945, 1175, 1241, 1243, 1739 as first written, 2344 and the Coptic versions without it, and Sinaiticus (01), P, 5, 436, 442, 1611, 1735, a corrector of 1739, 1852, 2492, the majority of manuscripts and the Syriac versions with it.
